source_refs.note: 6. Biosphere: a main subheading of Levels of Ecological Organization, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 229-230.

blocks.text: The biosphere is the highest and most inclusive level of ecological organization. It is the global sum of all biomes. It refers to every part of the Earth where life exists - from the deepest trenches of the Arabian Sea to the highest peaks of the Himalayas, and even several kilometers up into the atmosphere.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The biosphere is often called the "Global Ecosystem". It is a thin "envelope" around the Earth where the lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), and atmosphere (air) interact to support life.

blocks.alt: Six linked hexagons in two rows, as printed. Bottom row, left to right: 1. Species (an Indus River dolphin), 2. Population (several dolphins in muddy water), 3. Community (a pond with dolphins, fish, reeds and a heron). Top row, right to left: 4. Ecosystem (sun, rain cloud, mountains, forest and a river basin), 5. Biome (map of Pakistan with forest, desert and riverine zones), 6. Biosphere (the globe).
blocks.caption: Figure 25.1: Levels of ecological organization (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.1).
blocks.long_description: Panel texts: 1. SPECIES, Indus River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica minor), Defined by interbreeding and fertile offspring. 2. POPULATION, Indus River Dolphins, various, Same species in a defined area, e.g., Indus River. 3. COMMUNITY, Different populations interacting in one area. 4. ECOSYSTEM, Biotic Community + Abiotic Environment (e.g., Sindh River Basin), Energy Flow, Nutrient Cycling. 5. BIOME, Large regional unit defined by climate, CONIFEROUS FOREST (Swat), DESERT (Thar), RIVERINE (Indus). 6. BIOSPHERE, The entire zone of life on Earth, ATMOSPHERE, LITHOSPHERE, HYDROSPHERE, Global Ecosystem. Arrows lead from 1 to 2 to 3 along the bottom row, up from 3 to 4, and from 4 to 5 to 6 along the top row.
